system.name: Beehive
system.one_liner: an asynchronous runtime for memory-disaggregated servers that runs each application thread to completion via coroutine-based (pararoutine) execution instead of thread switching

content.subject: how synchronous thread-switching hides remote-memory latency compared to asynchronous coroutine execution on one thread

elements.name: Thread 1
elements.role: the thread that issues the remote memory access and later resumes on the fetched value

elements.name: Thread 2
elements.role: a second thread scheduled onto the CPU while Thread 1 is blocked on its remote access

elements.name: deref grid value
elements.role: thread dereferences a grid-point pointer, triggering a remote memory access

elements.name: post request
elements.role: thread posts the remote-memory read request

elements.name: save context
elements.role: runtime saves the blocked thread's context before switching away

elements.name: thread switching
elements.role: the CPU switches from the blocked thread to another ready thread

elements.name: in remote memory
elements.role: annotates the latency window during which the requested grid value is being fetched from remote memory

elements.name: poll request
elements.role: the other thread polls for completion of its own outstanding request

elements.name: restore context
elements.role: runtime restores the original thread's context once its remote data has arrived

elements.name: compute on grid value
elements.role: thread resumes and computes on the now-available grid value

relations.what: sequential execution before yielding the CPU
context is saved just before switching threads
CPU is handed to Thread 2, which polls its own pending request
once the remote fetch completes, Thread 1's context is restored
thread resumes and computes on the fetched value

panels.label: (a) Synchronous execution
panels.differs: template: two threads take turns on the CPU; the blocked thread's context is saved, another ready thread (Thread 2) is switched in while the remote access is outstanding, then context is restored to resume

panels.label: (b) Asynchronous execution
panels.differs: a single thread never switches out; it registers a callback continuation and keeps executing the next pararoutine's code, later polling events and restoring the continuation once the remote access finishes, overlapping the wait with useful work on the same thread

content.key_idea: Synchronous execution hides remote-memory latency by switching the CPU to a second thread, at the cost of saving/restoring context, while asynchronous execution keeps one thread running by registering a continuation and executing other coroutines' code, then resuming once the remote access completes.
content.reading_order: top to bottom within each panel; left panel (a) alternates between the Thread 1 and Thread 2 columns, right panel (b) reads straight down Thread 1's single column with the 'overlapping period' bracket at its centre

summary: Figure 1 of Beehive's background section contrasts synchronous and asynchronous ways to hide microsecond-scale remote-memory latency in multithreaded programs, using a Multi-Grid PDE traversal as the running example. Panel (a) shows synchronous execution: Thread 1 dereferences a grid value and posts a remote request, then saves its context and undergoes a thread switch so Thread 2 can run (polling its own request, saving context, switching again) while Thread 1's data is 'in remote memory'; once it returns, Thread 1's context is restored and it computes on the value. Panel (b) shows asynchronous execution: a single Thread 1 instead registers a callback continuation and continues executing the next pararoutine's code, later polling events and restoring the continuation once the access completes, so the wait overlaps with useful work on the same thread without ever switching threads. Colour-coded green/blue/orange boxes mark matching step types across both panels.
